written.q: 1. (a) "The roles of teachers and learners are influenced by interpersonal factors."—Elucidate.
written.a:
Interpersonal Factors and Classroom Roles

A classroom is not only a place where knowledge is passed on; it is a small society where people constantly interact. The way a teacher behaves and the way learners respond are shaped by interpersonal factors — the feelings, attitudes, expectations and relationships that exist between the people in the room. That is why the same teacher may play a different role with different classes, and the same learner may be active in one class and silent in another.

Key interpersonal factors that shape roles:

  • Teacher–student rapport: When a warm, trusting relationship exists, the teacher can act as a facilitator, guide and counsellor, and learners take on active roles — asking questions, volunteering and taking risks with the language. A cold or distant relationship pushes the teacher into the role of a controller and learners into passive receivers.
  • Attitudes and expectations: A teacher's expectation of a learner often becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy (the Pygmalion effect). Learners who are expected to do well are given more chances to speak and lead, so their role in the class grows.
  • Personality and emotions: Shy, anxious or introverted learners may avoid speaking roles, while confident learners may dominate. A sensitive teacher notices this and redistributes roles through pair and group work.
  • Peer relationships: Friendships, rivalries and group dynamics among learners decide who leads a group, who becomes the reporter and who stays silent. The teacher must manage these relationships to ensure equal participation.
  • Communication style: A teacher who listens, praises and gives feedback politely encourages learners to become partners in learning. Harsh correction makes learners fearful and dependent.
  • Cultural and social background: In many Bangladeshi classrooms, respect for the teacher means learners hesitate to question or disagree. The teacher has to consciously create a friendly atmosphere so learners can take on more communicative roles.

Example

In a CLT-based English class, the teacher sets a role-play. If the class trusts the teacher and each other, learners willingly take the roles of shopkeeper and customer, and the teacher steps back as a monitor. In a class with poor relationships, learners refuse to perform and the teacher is forced back into a lecturing role.

Conclusion: Roles in the classroom are not fixed by the syllabus alone; they grow out of human relationships. A teacher who builds rapport, shows empathy and manages group dynamics can move from controller to facilitator, and learners from passive listeners to active participants.

written.q: 1. (b) Discuss the common problems associated with social roles in a classroom environment.
written.a:
Common Problems Associated with Social Roles in the Classroom

Every member of a classroom takes on a social role — the teacher as leader and guide, learners as group members, leaders, helpers, or sometimes as jokers and trouble-makers. These roles help a class function, but they also create problems that a teacher must handle.

1. Problems related to the teacher's role

  • Role conflict: The teacher is expected to be a friend, a disciplinarian, an assessor and a counsellor at the same time. Being too friendly may weaken discipline; being too strict may destroy rapport.
  • Authoritarian dominance: When the teacher holds all control, learners become passive and communicative activities fail.
  • Favouritism: Giving more attention to bright or well-behaved learners makes others feel neglected and demotivated.

2. Problems related to learners' roles

  • Dominant learners: A few confident students take over discussions and group tasks, while others get no chance to speak.
  • Passive or withdrawn learners: Shy, anxious or weak learners hide behind others and avoid participation.
  • Negative roles: Some learners adopt the role of class clown, rebel or attention-seeker, which disrupts lessons.
  • Peer pressure and group conflict: Rivalry, bullying or exclusion of certain students makes pair and group work difficult.
  • Gender and social-status barriers: In mixed classes, girls or learners from poorer backgrounds may hesitate to speak in front of others.

3. Problems in the classroom environment

  • Large class size: It is hard to give everyone a role or notice who is excluded.
  • Cultural expectations: Learners used to teacher-centred classes may resist taking active roles such as group leader or presenter.
  • Lack of clear rules: If roles in group work (leader, writer, reporter, time-keeper) are not defined, a few students do all the work.

Ways to minimise these problems

  • Rotate roles in group work so that every learner gets to lead, write and report.
  • Use pair work and small groups to give shy learners a safe space to talk.
  • Set clear classroom rules together with the learners.
  • Treat all learners fairly and praise effort, not only ability.
  • Deal privately and positively with disruptive behaviour.

Conclusion: Social roles are natural in any classroom, but if they are left unmanaged they lead to dominance, exclusion and indiscipline. A skilful teacher balances these roles so that every learner feels valued and gets a fair chance to participate.

written.q: Or, (a) Discuss the concept of 'continuous assessment' and its advantages in a language classroom.
written.a:
Continuous Assessment

Continuous assessment is a system of evaluating learners' progress regularly throughout the course, instead of judging them only by a single final examination. Information is collected day by day through class work, homework, quizzes, oral tasks, projects, presentations and observation, and these results are used both to help learning and to build the final grade. In Bangladesh, it is known as ধারাবাহিক মূল্যায়ন and is a central part of the new competency-based curriculum.

Features of continuous assessment

  • It is ongoing and regular — it happens during the teaching–learning process.
  • It is comprehensive — it covers all four skills (listening, speaking, reading, writing) as well as attitudes and participation.
  • It uses a variety of tools — observation, checklists, rubrics, portfolios, peer and self-assessment.
  • It is mainly formative — feedback is given immediately so learners can improve.

Advantages in a language classroom

  • Assesses all skills: A written final exam cannot test speaking and listening properly; continuous assessment can assess them through role-plays, dialogues and listening tasks.
  • Immediate feedback: Errors in grammar, pronunciation or spelling are identified early and corrected before they become fossilised.
  • Reduces exam anxiety: Since the grade does not depend on one exam, learners feel less stress and use the language more freely.
  • Encourages regular study: Learners stay active throughout the term instead of memorising before the exam.
  • Helps the teacher: The teacher gets ongoing information about which methods work and can adjust the lesson plan.
  • Supports weak learners: Learning gaps are found early and remedial teaching can be given.
  • More valid and reliable picture: Many observations over time give a fairer judgement of a learner's real language ability than one test.
  • Promotes learner autonomy: Self and peer assessment help learners reflect on their own progress.

Conclusion: Continuous assessment turns assessment into a part of learning. In a language classroom, where skills develop gradually through practice, it is far more effective than relying only on terminal examinations.

written.q: Or, (b) Define 'Reliability' and 'Validity'. Why are these issues important in language testing?
written.a:
Reliability

Reliability is the consistency of a test. A test is reliable if it gives the same or nearly the same results when it is taken again under similar conditions, or when it is scored by different examiners. For example, if a student scores 70 on a grammar test today and about 70 on the same test next week, the test is reliable.

Factors affecting reliability: clear instructions, length of the test, objective scoring keys, trained examiners, and similar test conditions.

Validity

Validity is the extent to which a test measures what it is supposed to measure. A speaking test that only asks students to write sentences is not valid, because it does not measure speaking ability.

Main types: content validity (covers the syllabus), construct validity (measures the intended skill or ability), face validity (looks appropriate to test-takers) and criterion/predictive validity (results agree with other measures or predict future performance).

Why are reliability and validity important in language testing?

  • Fair decisions: Test results are used for promotion, placement, certification and admission. Unreliable or invalid tests lead to unfair decisions about learners.
  • Measuring real language ability: Language is a complex skill. Without validity, a test may measure memory or general knowledge instead of reading, writing, listening or speaking.
  • Consistency in subjective scoring: Essays and speaking tests are often scored subjectively. Reliability (using rubrics, multiple raters) ensures that the grade depends on the learner's performance, not on the examiner's mood.
  • Positive washback: A valid test that assesses communicative skills encourages teachers and learners to practise those skills in class.
  • Useful feedback for teaching: Teachers can trust the results to identify weaknesses and plan remedial lessons.
  • Credibility of the system: Public examinations like SSC, HSC or IELTS must be reliable and valid so that society trusts the results.

Relationship between the two

A test must be reliable to be valid, but a reliable test is not always valid. For instance, a spelling test may give consistent results (reliable) but it is not a valid test of speaking ability. Therefore, a good language test must have both qualities.

written.q: 2. (a) Describe the characteristics of a good teacher.
written.a:
Characteristics of a Good Teacher

A good teacher is someone who not only knows the subject but also knows how to make learners learn. The characteristics of a good teacher, especially a good English language teacher, can be grouped as follows:

A. Professional qualities

  • Command over the subject: Good knowledge of English grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation and literature, and the ability to use the language fluently.
  • Knowledge of methods: Familiarity with CLT, GTM, Direct Method, inductive and deductive approaches, and the ability to choose suitable methods.
  • Lesson planning: Prepares lessons with clear learning outcomes, activities and assessment.
  • Classroom management: Maintains discipline, manages time, organises pair and group work smoothly.
  • Use of teaching aids and ICT: Uses boards, pictures, realia, audio-visual materials and multimedia effectively.
  • Assessment skills: Uses formative and summative assessment and gives constructive feedback.

B. Personal qualities

  • Patience and empathy: Understands that learners learn at different speeds and makes mistakes.
  • Friendliness and approachability: Learners feel free to ask questions.
  • Enthusiasm: Shows passion for teaching, which motivates learners.
  • Fairness and impartiality: Treats all learners equally, without favouritism.
  • Sense of humour: Makes the classroom relaxed and enjoyable.
  • Good personality and appearance: Neat, punctual, confident and a role model.

C. Communicative qualities

  • Clear voice, correct pronunciation and simple instructions.
  • Active listening and the ability to encourage learners to speak.
  • Good use of body language, gestures and eye contact.

D. Reflective and lifelong learner

  • Reflects on his/her own teaching and improves it.
  • Participates in training, workshops and professional development.
  • Is open to feedback from learners, colleagues and supervisors.

E. Social and moral qualities

  • Maintains good relations with parents and the community.
  • Has honesty, integrity and respect for learners' dignity.

Conclusion: A good teacher is a combination of knowledge, skill and personality. He or she acts as a guide, facilitator and motivator who helps learners become confident users of the language.

written.q: 2. (b) What kind of relationship do you consider as the ideal relationship between teachers and students? Why?
written.a:
The Ideal Teacher–Student Relationship

In my opinion, the ideal relationship between a teacher and students is a friendly yet respectful, guide–learner relationship — often described as "friendly but not familiar". The teacher should be approachable like a friend and caring like a parent, but should also keep enough authority to maintain discipline and respect.

Features of the ideal relationship

  • Mutual respect: The teacher respects learners' feelings, opinions and dignity; learners respect the teacher's knowledge and guidance.
  • Trust and rapport: Learners trust that the teacher will help, not humiliate, them when they make mistakes.
  • Open communication: Learners can ask questions, express doubts and share problems freely.
  • Care and empathy: The teacher understands learners' backgrounds, difficulties and individual needs.
  • Fairness: All learners are treated equally regardless of ability, gender or social status.
  • Professional boundary: Friendliness does not mean losing control; rules and expectations remain clear.
  • Partnership in learning: The teacher acts as a facilitator and guide, and learners are active partners, not passive listeners.

Why is this relationship ideal?

  • Lowers the affective filter: According to Krashen, learners acquire language best when anxiety is low. A friendly teacher reduces fear, so learners speak English more freely.
  • Increases motivation: Learners who like and trust their teacher work harder and enjoy the subject.
  • Supports CLT: Communicative activities like role-play, pair work and discussion need a relaxed and cooperative atmosphere.
  • Better discipline: Respect, rather than fear, leads to self-discipline; learners follow rules willingly.
  • Effective feedback: Learners accept correction positively when they know the teacher cares for them.
  • Holistic development: The teacher can guide learners morally and emotionally, not only academically.

Conclusion: A relationship based on mutual respect, trust and care — where the teacher is a friend, philosopher and guide — creates the best environment for language learning and personal growth.

written.q: Or, (a) What is reflection? How does a trainee teacher practice reflection?
written.a:
Reflection

Reflection in teaching means thinking carefully and critically about one's own teaching experiences — what happened in the class, why it happened, how effective it was and how it can be improved. John Dewey described reflective thinking as "active, persistent and careful consideration of any belief or practice." Donald Schön divided it into reflection-in-action (thinking while teaching and adjusting immediately) and reflection-on-action (thinking after the lesson).

A reflective teacher does not repeat the same lesson mechanically; he or she learns from experience and keeps improving.

The reflective cycle

Plan → Teach → Observe/collect information → Reflect (analyse) → Revise the plan → Teach again.

How a trainee teacher practises reflection

  • Keeping a reflective journal/diary: After each practice teaching lesson, the trainee writes what went well, what problems occurred and what can be done differently.
  • Self-evaluation checklists: Using a checklist on lesson planning, presentation, questioning, use of aids, time management and classroom management.
  • Feedback from supervisors: Discussing the lesson with the college supervisor or the school's subject teacher and noting the suggestions.
  • Peer observation: Fellow trainees observe each other's lessons and share honest feedback.
  • Learner feedback: Asking students what they enjoyed or found difficult, or checking their performance in the evaluation part of the lesson.
  • Audio/video recording: Recording a lesson and watching it later to notice voice, body language, teacher talk time and errors.
  • Micro-teaching: Practising one skill at a time (e.g., questioning) and re-teaching after feedback.
  • Action research: Identifying a classroom problem (e.g., students do not speak English), trying a solution and reflecting on its effect.
  • Portfolio: Collecting lesson plans, materials, feedback and reflections to see personal growth over time.

Conclusion: Reflection turns experience into learning. Through regular reflection, a trainee teacher identifies strengths and weaknesses and gradually develops into a confident, effective professional.

written.q: Or, (b) What do you mean by active and passive vocabulary? What are the stages of presenting a new word?
written.a:
Active and Passive Vocabulary

Active (productive) vocabulary is the set of words a learner can understand and use correctly in speaking and writing. For example, a class six learner can use words like book, school, play, happy in their own sentences.

Passive (receptive) vocabulary is the set of words a learner recognises and understands when listening or reading but cannot yet use confidently. For example, a learner may understand enormous or reluctant in a story but may not use them while speaking.

Active vocabularyPassive vocabulary
Used in speaking and writingRecognised in listening and reading
Smaller in sizeLarger in size
Needs more practiceNeeds exposure
Productive skillReceptive skill

A teacher's aim is to turn useful passive words into active ones through repeated practice.

Stages of Presenting a New Word

  1. Presentation of form (sound and spelling): The teacher says the word clearly several times, the class repeats chorally and individually, and then the teacher writes it on the board, marking stress if needed.
  2. Presentation of meaning: Meaning is made clear using suitable techniques — visual (realia, picture, mime, gesture, model) or verbal (example sentence, definition, synonym/antonym, context). Translation is used only as a last resort.
  3. Checking understanding: The teacher asks concept-checking questions, e.g., for honest: "Does an honest man tell lies?"
  4. Use in context / practice: The word is shown in model sentences, and learners make their own sentences, fill gaps, match words with pictures or use them in dialogues.
  5. Consolidation and recording: Learners copy the word with meaning and an example in their vocabulary notebook, and the word is revised in later lessons.

Example: presenting "umbrella"

The teacher shows a real umbrella (realia), says "umbrella" (/ʌmˈbrelə/), learners repeat; the word is written on the board with stress on the second syllable; the teacher asks "When do we use an umbrella?" and learners make sentences like "I take an umbrella on a rainy day."

written.q: 3. (a) What is correct pronunciation? Mention some impacts of poor or bad pronunciation.
written.a:
Correct Pronunciation

Correct pronunciation means producing the sounds of a language — its vowels, consonants, word stress, sentence stress, rhythm and intonation — in a way that is clear, intelligible and acceptable to other speakers of that language. In English language teaching, the target is not necessarily a "perfect native accent" but intelligibility: the speaker should be easily understood by listeners from different backgrounds. Standard models such as Received Pronunciation (RP) or General American are usually used as references.

Elements of correct pronunciation

  • Segmental features: correct vowel sounds (e.g., /ɪ/ in ship vs /iː/ in sheep) and consonant sounds (e.g., /v/ vs /b/, /z/ vs /dʒ/).
  • Supra-segmental features: correct word stress (PHOtograph, phoTOgraphy), sentence stress, rhythm, intonation and connected speech.

Impacts of poor or bad pronunciation

  • Misunderstanding of meaning: Minimal pair confusion changes meaning — ship/sheep, live/leave, very/berry. Wrong stress can also change meaning (REcord noun vs reCORD verb).
  • Communication breakdown: Listeners may not understand the message at all, especially in international communication.
  • Loss of confidence: Learners who are laughed at for poor pronunciation become shy and avoid speaking.
  • Weak listening skills: If learners pronounce words wrongly, they often fail to recognise the same words when native speakers say them.
  • Negative impression: In interviews, presentations and jobs, poor pronunciation may create an impression of low proficiency even when grammar and vocabulary are good.
  • Spread of errors: A teacher with poor pronunciation passes the same errors on to hundreds of learners, and these errors become fossilised.
  • Spelling problems: Wrong pronunciation can lead to wrong spelling and vice versa.
  • Lower scores: In speaking tests such as IELTS, pronunciation is a scoring criterion.

Conclusion: Correct pronunciation is essential for intelligible and confident communication. Therefore, teachers should model correct pronunciation and give learners regular practice.

written.q: 3. (b) As an English teacher, how will you teach pronunciation in the class?
written.a:
Teaching Pronunciation in the Classroom

Pronunciation should not be taught as a separate, boring drill; it should be integrated with listening and speaking activities. As an English teacher, I would follow the steps and techniques below.

1. Be a good model

  • Pronounce words and sentences clearly and correctly myself.
  • Use audio/video recordings of native or fluent speakers (dictionary audio, BBC Learning English, textbook CDs).

2. Listening and discrimination

  • Let learners listen carefully before they speak — "ear before mouth".
  • Minimal pair practice: ship–sheep, fan–van, sit–seat, very–berry. Learners identify which word they hear.

3. Imitation and drilling

  • Choral drill: The whole class repeats after the teacher.
  • Group and individual drill: Then smaller groups and individuals repeat, so I can identify errors.
  • Back-chaining for long words or sentences: -tion → -cation → education.

4. Teaching sounds explicitly

  • Show how sounds are made — position of tongue, lips and teeth (e.g., /θ/ in think: tongue between teeth).
  • Use a phonemic chart and simple IPA symbols for difficult sounds.
  • Focus on sounds that are problematic for Bangladeshi learners: /v/–/b/, /z/–/dʒ/, /ʃ/–/s/, /æ/, /ɜː/, and final consonant clusters.

5. Teaching stress and intonation

  • Mark word stress on the board with dots or capital letters: teaCHER → TEAcher.
  • Use clapping or tapping to show sentence rhythm.
  • Use arrows to show rising and falling intonation in questions and statements.

6. Meaningful practice

  • Dialogues, role-plays, reading aloud, tongue twisters, songs, rhymes and short poems.
  • Pair work where learners correct each other's pronunciation.

7. Correction and feedback

  • Correct errors gently and at the right time — during accuracy activities, not in the middle of fluency activities.
  • Use techniques like recasting, finger correction and self-correction.

8. Use of technology

  • Online dictionaries with audio, recording apps so learners can record and compare their voice with a model.

Conclusion: By combining good modelling, listening practice, drilling, explicit teaching of sounds and stress, and meaningful communicative practice, I can help learners develop clear and intelligible pronunciation.

written.q: 4. (a) Describe different possible ways of making necessary correction while teaching speaking in the classroom.
written.a:
Ways of Correcting Errors While Teaching Speaking

Error correction in speaking must be handled carefully. Too much correction discourages learners and kills fluency; too little allows errors to fossilise. The teacher must decide what to correct, when to correct and how to correct.

When to correct

  • Accuracy activities (drills, controlled practice): correct immediately.
  • Fluency activities (discussion, role-play): do not interrupt; note errors and correct later (delayed correction).
  • Correct errors that affect meaning (global errors) before minor ones (local errors).

Techniques of correction

  • Self-correction: The teacher signals that there is a mistake (a questioning look, "Again?", "Almost!") and the learner corrects it himself. This is the best option.
  • Peer correction: If the learner cannot correct it, the teacher asks another learner: "Can anyone help?"
  • Teacher correction: If no one can, the teacher gives the correct form and the learner repeats it.
  • Recasting: The teacher repeats the learner's sentence correctly without pointing out the error directly. Student: "He go to school." Teacher: "Oh, he goes to school every day?"
  • Echoing / repetition with rising intonation: "He go?" — highlighting the error.
  • Finger correction: Each finger represents a word; the teacher points to the finger where the mistake is (useful for missing words or wrong word order).
  • Gesture and facial expression: Hand behind ear for pronunciation, pointing backward for past tense, etc.
  • Elicitation: The teacher pauses and lets the learner complete: "Yesterday he ...?"
  • Metalinguistic clue: "Remember, third person singular takes -s."
  • Delayed / group correction: The teacher notes common errors during the activity and writes them on the board afterwards without naming learners; the class corrects them together.
  • Recording: Recording speaking tasks so learners can hear and correct their own errors.

Principles to follow

  • Be positive, polite and encouraging; praise before correcting.
  • Never humiliate a learner in front of the class.
  • Do not correct every single error; focus on the target language of the lesson.

Conclusion: Effective correction balances accuracy with fluency. By using self-correction, peer correction, recasting, gestures and delayed correction, the teacher can improve learners' speaking without reducing their confidence.

written.q: 4. (b) As an English teacher, how can you use blackboard or whiteboard effectively in the classroom?
written.a:
Effective Use of the Blackboard/Whiteboard

The blackboard or whiteboard is the most common, cheapest and most flexible teaching aid. Used well, it helps learners see, organise and remember the lesson. As an English teacher, I would use it in the following ways.

A. Planning and organising the board

  • Divide the board: Keep a left section for date, topic and learning outcomes; a large middle section for main teaching points; a right section for new vocabulary and quick notes.
  • Plan the board layout before the class as part of the lesson plan.
  • Write the topic and date clearly at the top.

B. Writing techniques

  • Write in large, clear and legible handwriting that can be read from the back bench.
  • Write in straight lines from left to right and top to bottom.
  • Use coloured chalk/markers to highlight key words, tense forms, stress or spelling patterns.
  • Stand at an angle so that learners can see what you write; do not hide the board with your body.
  • Do not talk to the board for a long time; keep eye contact with the class.
  • Use correct spelling and punctuation — learners copy what they see.

C. Uses in English teaching

  • Vocabulary: Write new words with meaning, part of speech, stress mark and an example sentence.
  • Grammar: Show structures with tables, timelines and formulas (e.g., Subject + was/were + V-ing).
  • Pronunciation: Mark stress and intonation with dots, underlines and arrows.
  • Writing skills: Model a paragraph, letter or dialogue step by step; brainstorm ideas with mind maps.
  • Reading: Write pre-reading questions and key words.
  • Simple drawings: Stick figures and sketches to explain meaning quickly.
  • Games: Word puzzles, hangman, crosswords to review vocabulary.
  • Learner participation: Invite learners to write answers or correct sentences on the board.

D. Good practices

  • Erase unnecessary writing to avoid clutter; keep the board clean.
  • Leave the summary on the board at the end so learners can copy it.
  • Combine the board with other aids such as pictures and flashcards stuck on it.

Conclusion: A well-organised board acts as a visual summary of the lesson. With planned layout, clear writing, use of colour and active learner involvement, the board becomes a powerful tool in the English classroom.

written.q: 5. (a) What is meant by self-evaluation? Discuss.
written.a:
Self-evaluation

Self-evaluation is the process by which a person examines and judges his or her own performance, learning or behaviour against certain standards or goals. In education, it applies to both teachers (evaluating their own teaching) and learners (evaluating their own learning). It is closely linked with reflective teaching and Assessment as Learning.

Self-evaluation for the teacher

A teacher asks questions such as: Did I achieve the learning outcomes? Were my instructions clear? Did all learners participate? Was the time well used? What should I change next time?

Tools: reflective journal, self-evaluation checklist, lesson recording, learner feedback, peer observation, portfolio.

Self-evaluation for learners

Learners judge their own work using checklists, rubrics, "can-do" statements (e.g., "I can introduce myself in English"), learning logs and portfolios. For example, after writing a paragraph, a learner checks: Is there a topic sentence? Are the tenses correct? Did I use capital letters and full stops?

Steps of self-evaluation

  1. Set clear goals or criteria.
  2. Perform the task or teach the lesson.
  3. Collect evidence (work samples, recordings, results).
  4. Compare performance with the criteria.
  5. Identify strengths and weaknesses.
  6. Plan and apply improvements.

Importance / advantages

  • Promotes learner autonomy and responsibility for one's own learning.
  • Develops critical thinking and metacognitive skills.
  • Helps teachers improve continuously and grow professionally.
  • Increases motivation, as learners see their own progress.
  • Reduces dependence on the teacher for every correction.
  • Supports continuous assessment in the new curriculum.

Limitations

  • It can be subjective; people may over- or under-rate themselves.
  • Learners need training and clear criteria to evaluate themselves honestly.

Therefore, self-evaluation works best when combined with teacher and peer evaluation.

written.q: 5. (b) What is a 'Mixed Ability Class'? Mention the challenges a teacher faces in such a classroom.
written.a:
Mixed Ability Class

A mixed ability class is a class in which learners differ widely in their level of language proficiency, learning speed, intelligence, background knowledge, motivation and learning styles. In fact, every class is mixed to some extent, but in a mixed ability class the differences are large — some learners can speak English fluently while others can hardly read a simple sentence. Most classes in Bangladeshi schools are mixed ability classes.

Sources of difference

  • Language level and previous learning
  • Speed of learning and intelligence
  • Learning styles (visual, auditory, kinaesthetic)
  • Motivation, interest and attitude
  • Socio-economic and family background, access to private tuition or technology
  • Personality — confident vs shy learners

Challenges a teacher faces

  • Choosing the level of teaching: If the lesson is pitched at the average, advanced learners get bored and weak learners get lost.
  • Pace of the lesson: Fast learners finish early and become restless; slow learners cannot finish.
  • Selecting materials: One textbook cannot suit everyone; the teacher must adapt or prepare extra materials.
  • Unequal participation: Strong learners dominate; weak learners stay silent and lose confidence.
  • Classroom management: Bored or frustrated learners may create discipline problems.
  • Assessment: It is difficult to design tests that are fair to all levels.
  • Motivation: Weak learners may feel inferior; strong learners may feel unchallenged.
  • Individual attention: With large classes and limited time, giving attention to everyone is very difficult.
  • Workload: Planning differentiated tasks requires more time and effort.

Possible solutions (briefly)

  • Differentiated tasks (same text, different questions; open-ended tasks).
  • Pair and group work mixing strong and weak learners (peer tutoring).
  • Extra tasks for fast finishers and support for slow learners.
  • Variety of activities to suit different learning styles.
  • Encouraging and praising effort, not only results.

written.q: 1. (a) Do you think pair work and group work help teachers to make EFL classroom more student centric? Explain your opinion.
written.a:
Pair Work and Group Work in a Student-Centred EFL Classroom

Yes, I strongly believe that pair work and group work help teachers make an EFL (English as a Foreign Language) classroom more student-centric. In a traditional teacher-centred class, the teacher talks most of the time and learners only listen. In pair and group work, the focus shifts from the teacher to the learners: they talk, share, solve problems and learn from each other, while the teacher becomes a facilitator and monitor.

Reasons in support of my opinion

  • More student talking time (STT): In a class of 60, if the teacher asks questions one by one, each learner may speak for only a few seconds. In pair work, half the class speaks at the same time, so every learner gets much more practice.
  • Real communication: Role-plays, interviews, information-gap tasks and discussions create genuine reasons to use English, which is the main aim of CLT.
  • Reduced anxiety: Shy and weak learners feel safer speaking to a partner or a small group than in front of the whole class. This lowers the affective filter.
  • Peer learning: Stronger learners help weaker ones; learners correct and explain to each other, which deepens understanding for both.
  • Learner responsibility and autonomy: Learners plan, decide and complete tasks themselves instead of waiting for the teacher's answers.
  • Development of social skills: Cooperation, turn-taking, leadership, tolerance and respect for others' opinions develop naturally.
  • Higher motivation: Activities are interactive and enjoyable, so learners stay engaged.
  • Teacher as facilitator: The teacher moves around, monitors, helps and notes common errors for later feedback — a truly student-centred role.

Example

In a lesson on "Asking for directions", learners work in pairs with a simple map. Learner A asks, "How can I go to the post office?" and Learner B gives directions. Then they swap roles. Every learner speaks, listens and negotiates meaning.

Conditions for success

Clear instructions, a time limit, defined roles in groups, suitable seating and proper monitoring are needed; otherwise noise and use of the mother tongue may increase.

Conclusion: When planned and managed well, pair work and group work transform the EFL classroom into an active, communicative and learner-centred place.

written.q: 1. (b) What is competency? Write the expected competencies of a secondary English teacher.
written.a:
Competency

Competency is the combination of knowledge, skills, attitudes and values that enables a person to perform a task or job effectively in real-life situations. A competent teacher not only knows the subject but can also apply that knowledge to help learners learn. Bangladesh's new curriculum (2021) is competency-based, so teachers are expected to develop learners' competencies through experiential learning.

Expected Competencies of a Secondary English Teacher

1. Language proficiency

  • Fluency and accuracy in all four skills — listening, speaking, reading and writing.
  • Correct pronunciation, grammar and a rich vocabulary.

2. Subject and pedagogical knowledge

  • Knowledge of the national curriculum, textbook and learning outcomes.
  • Knowledge of methods and approaches: CLT, GTM, Direct Method, inductive/deductive grammar teaching.
  • Ability to teach the four skills integrally.

3. Planning skills

  • Preparing annual, unit and daily lesson plans with SMART learning outcomes.
  • Selecting suitable activities, materials and assessment techniques.

4. Classroom management skills

  • Organising pair and group work, managing large and mixed-ability classes, maintaining discipline and time.

5. Communication and interpersonal skills

  • Giving clear instructions, asking good questions, active listening and building rapport with learners.

6. Use of teaching aids and ICT

  • Using the board, pictures, realia, audio-visual materials, multimedia and online resources effectively.

7. Assessment skills

  • Designing valid and reliable tests, using formative and summative assessment, giving constructive feedback and keeping records.

8. Professional development and reflection

  • Reflecting on own teaching, participating in training, action research and peer observation.

9. Personal and ethical qualities

  • Patience, empathy, fairness, punctuality, honesty and respect for learners' dignity.

These competencies together help a secondary English teacher create an effective, communicative and inclusive learning environment.

written.q: Or, (a) What is assessment? Describe formative and summative assessment in detail.
written.a:
Assessment

Assessment is the systematic process of collecting, analysing and interpreting information about learners' learning in order to know how well they are achieving the intended learning outcomes and to make decisions for improving teaching and learning. It includes tests, quizzes, observation, homework, projects, presentations and portfolios.

Formative Assessment

Formative assessment is the ongoing assessment carried out during the teaching–learning process to monitor learners' progress and to improve learning. It is known as Assessment for Learning.

Features

  • Continuous and regular; takes place throughout a lesson or unit.
  • Gives immediate feedback to learners and teachers.
  • Usually low-stakes — not used mainly for final grades.
  • Helps identify learning gaps and plan remedial teaching.

Tools/examples: oral questions, class work, quizzes, homework, observation checklists, peer and self-assessment, exit cards, short writing tasks.

Summative Assessment

Summative assessment is carried out at the end of a unit, term, course or year to measure how much learners have achieved. It is known as Assessment of Learning.

Features

  • Takes place at the end of instruction.
  • High-stakes — used for grading, promotion and certification.
  • Covers a large part of the syllabus.
  • Feedback for improvement is limited.

Examples: half-yearly and annual examinations, SSC/HSC, final project grades.

Comparison

PointFormativeSummative
TimeDuring learningEnd of learning
PurposeImprove learningJudge/certify achievement
FeedbackImmediateDelayed/limited
StakesLowHigh
ExampleQuiz, class workAnnual exam, SSC

Both are necessary: formative assessment improves learning, and summative assessment shows the final level of achievement.

written.q: Or, (b) What is your understanding about Assessment For Learning (AFL)? Explain your thoughts.
written.a:
Assessment for Learning (AfL)

Assessment for Learning (AfL) is the use of assessment during teaching to find out where learners are in their learning, where they need to go, and how best to get there. Its main aim is not to give marks but to improve learning. The Assessment Reform Group (2002) defined it as "the process of seeking and interpreting evidence for use by learners and their teachers to decide where the learners are in their learning, where they need to go and how best to get there." AfL is another name for formative assessment.

Key principles/strategies of AfL

  • Sharing learning outcomes and success criteria: Learners know what they are learning and what a good performance looks like.
  • Effective questioning: Open and thought-provoking questions reveal learners' understanding.
  • Constructive feedback: Specific, timely comments that tell learners how to improve, not just a score.
  • Peer assessment: Learners check each other's work using criteria.
  • Self-assessment: Learners reflect on their own progress.
  • Using assessment information to adjust teaching: The teacher changes the plan, re-teaches or gives extra support where needed.

My thoughts on AfL

  • AfL makes assessment a part of learning, not something separate at the end.
  • It is especially useful in English teaching, where skills develop gradually; errors in pronunciation, grammar and writing can be corrected early.
  • It reduces exam fear and builds learners' confidence, because mistakes are treated as chances to learn.
  • It encourages learner autonomy — learners become responsible for their own learning.
  • It helps the teacher reflect and become more effective.
  • It fits perfectly with Bangladesh's new competency-based curriculum, which emphasises continuous assessment.

Example

After a writing lesson, the teacher gives a checklist (topic sentence, supporting ideas, correct tense, punctuation). Learners check their partner's paragraph, then revise their own. The teacher notes common errors and re-teaches them next day.

Conclusion: In my view, AfL is one of the most powerful tools for raising achievement because it focuses on improvement, feedback and active learner involvement.

written.q: 2. (a) Why lesson plan is important for a teacher? What problems may arise in an unplanned lesson?
written.a:
Importance of a Lesson Plan

A lesson plan is a teacher's written guide for a particular lesson, stating learning outcomes, content, activities, materials, time and assessment. It is important because:

  • Clear direction: The teacher knows exactly what learners should achieve and how.
  • Logical sequence: Activities move from easy to difficult, known to unknown (e.g., warm-up → presentation → practice → production → evaluation).
  • Time management: Each stage gets proper time, so the lesson is completed.
  • Selection of methods and materials: Suitable techniques and aids are prepared in advance.
  • Confidence: A prepared teacher teaches with confidence and handles questions better.
  • Learner engagement: Varied activities keep learners active and motivated.
  • Addressing individual differences: The teacher can plan support for weak learners and extra tasks for fast learners.
  • Assessment: The teacher can check whether learning outcomes have been achieved.
  • Record and reflection: Plans help the teacher reflect, improve and maintain continuity; a substitute teacher can also use them.

Problems in an Unplanned Lesson

  • Lack of clear objectives: The teacher and learners do not know what is to be achieved.
  • Poor time management: Too much time on one part, while important parts are skipped.
  • Disorganised presentation: Ideas are presented randomly, causing confusion.
  • Repetition and gaps: Some content is repeated, some is missed.
  • Inappropriate methods: The teacher falls back on lecturing; learners become passive.
  • No teaching aids: Necessary materials are not prepared.
  • Discipline problems: Bored learners become restless and noisy.
  • Loss of confidence: The teacher may get stuck or nervous with unexpected questions.
  • No proper assessment: Learning cannot be checked, so weaknesses remain unidentified.
  • Wastage of learners' time and poor results.

Conclusion: A lesson plan is like a map for a journey. Without it, both teacher and learners may lose their way.

written.q: 2. (b) Do you think reflective teaching improves teacher's teaching? Explain your own views.
written.a:
Reflective Teaching and Teacher Improvement

Yes, I firmly believe that reflective teaching improves a teacher's teaching. Reflective teaching is a process in which teachers regularly think about their classroom practice — what they did, why they did it, whether it worked, and how it can be improved — and then make changes. As Dewey and Schön showed, learning from experience requires careful reflection, not just experience itself.

The reflective cycle

Teach → Observe/collect information → Reflect and analyse → Plan changes → Teach again.

My views on how reflective teaching improves teaching

  • Self-awareness: Teachers recognise their strengths and weaknesses — e.g., too much teacher talk, unclear instructions, ignoring back benchers.
  • Better decision-making: Teachers choose methods and activities based on evidence of what works with their learners, not on habit.
  • Learner-centred teaching: Reflection on learners' responses helps teachers adapt lessons to learners' needs, levels and interests.
  • Continuous professional development: Teachers keep learning throughout their career without depending only on formal training.
  • Problem solving: Classroom problems such as low participation or poor writing can be studied and solved through action research.
  • Confidence and job satisfaction: Seeing improvement motivates the teacher.
  • Avoiding routine teaching: Reflection prevents mechanical, repetitive lessons.

Tools of reflection

Teaching journals, lesson recordings, peer observation, learner feedback, self-evaluation checklists, portfolios and action research.

Example

A teacher notices that learners are silent during speaking activities. After reflecting, she realises the tasks are too difficult and learners fear mistakes. She introduces pair work and simpler tasks with useful phrases on the board. Participation increases — a direct result of reflection.

Conclusion: Reflective teaching turns everyday experience into professional growth. A reflective teacher becomes more effective every day, and learners benefit the most.

written.q: Or, (a) What is motivation? Discuss it's impact on foreign language acquisition.
written.a:
Motivation

Motivation is the inner drive or desire that makes a person start, continue and put effort into an activity to achieve a goal. In language learning, motivation is the learner's willingness and effort to learn the language. Gardner described it as the combination of effort, desire to achieve the goal, and positive attitude towards learning the language.

Types of motivation

  • Intrinsic motivation: Learning for interest and enjoyment (e.g., loving English songs and stories).
  • Extrinsic motivation: Learning for outside rewards (marks, jobs, praise, going abroad).
  • Integrative motivation: Wanting to communicate with and become part of the target-language community.
  • Instrumental motivation: Learning for practical benefits such as passing exams or getting a job.

Impact of Motivation on Foreign Language Acquisition

  • More effort and persistence: Motivated learners practise more, do homework regularly and do not give up when English becomes difficult.
  • Active participation: They volunteer to speak, ask questions and take part in pair and group activities, getting more practice.
  • Lower anxiety: Motivated learners are more confident and less afraid of mistakes, so the affective filter (Krashen) is low and input becomes intake.
  • More exposure: They read English books, watch films and listen to English outside the classroom, increasing comprehensible input.
  • Better achievement: Research shows motivation is one of the strongest predictors of success in second/foreign language learning.
  • Learner autonomy: Motivated learners set goals and take responsibility for their own learning.
  • Long-term retention: Intrinsically motivated learning lasts longer.

Lack of motivation leads to boredom, absence, low participation and poor results.

How teachers can increase motivation

Interesting, relevant materials; varied communicative activities; praise and positive feedback; achievable tasks; a friendly classroom; using songs, games, stories and ICT; and showing the real-life value of English.

written.q: Or, (b) "Audio-visual aids are helpful for learning foreign language"—Justify the statement.
written.a:
Audio-Visual Aids in Foreign Language Learning

Audio-visual aids are teaching materials that appeal to learners' senses of hearing and/or sight — such as pictures, charts, flashcards, realia, models, audio recordings, videos, films, multimedia presentations and computers. The statement is fully justified because such aids make foreign language learning easier, more meaningful and more enjoyable.

Justification

  • Make meaning clear: Pictures, objects and videos show the meaning of new words and situations directly, reducing the need for translation.
  • Authentic language input: Audio and video recordings expose learners to native/fluent speakers' pronunciation, stress, intonation and natural speed — something a textbook cannot provide.
  • Improve listening and speaking: Learners listen to dialogues and then imitate, role-play or discuss what they watched.
  • Context and culture: Videos show how language is used in real situations and introduce the culture of English-speaking communities.
  • Motivation and attention: Colourful visuals, songs and films attract learners' attention and make lessons lively.
  • Better retention: According to Edgar Dale's Cone of Experience, people remember much more of what they see and hear than of what they only read.
  • Address different learning styles: Visual and auditory learners both benefit.
  • Save time: A single picture or short clip can explain what would take many words.
  • Encourage communication: Pictures and videos provide topics for description, discussion and story-writing.
  • Support weak and young learners: Concrete aids help them understand abstract language.

Examples

  • Flashcards and realia to teach vocabulary (fruits, vegetables).
  • Audio dialogue for a listening comprehension task.
  • A short video on "Traffic jam in Dhaka" followed by a discussion.
  • Picture series for story writing.

Caution

Aids must be relevant to the learning outcome, clear, appropriate to learners' level and used purposefully — not just for decoration.

Conclusion: Since audio-visual aids make input comprehensible, authentic, memorable and enjoyable, they are truly helpful for learning a foreign language.

written.q: 3. (a) What is competency?
written.a:
Competency

Competency is the ability to apply an integrated set of knowledge, skills, attitudes and values to perform a task successfully in a real-life context. It is not just knowing something, but being able to do it effectively and responsibly.

Formula often used in Bangladesh's new curriculum:

Competency = Knowledge + Skills + Attitudes + Values

Features of competency

  • Integrated: combines knowing, doing and being.
  • Observable and measurable: shown through performance.
  • Context-based: applied in real-life situations, not only in exams.
  • Developmental: grows gradually through practice and experience.
  • Transferable: can be used in new situations.

Examples

  • Learner competency: "Learners can write a formal application to the headteacher using appropriate format and language."
  • Teacher competency: "The teacher can plan and conduct a communicative lesson using pair and group work."

The national curriculum 2021 of Bangladesh is a competency-based curriculum; it focuses on what learners can do with their learning through experiential activities, rather than only memorising content.

written.q: 3. (b) What are the major competencies that an English teacher should have?
written.a:
Major Competencies of an English Teacher

An effective English teacher needs a range of competencies that combine language knowledge, teaching skills and professional attitudes.

1. Language competency

  • High proficiency in listening, speaking, reading and writing.
  • Accurate grammar, wide vocabulary, correct pronunciation, stress and intonation.

2. Pedagogical competency

  • Knowledge of ELT methods and approaches (CLT, GTM, Direct Method, Task-Based Learning).
  • Ability to teach the four skills, grammar (inductive/deductive) and vocabulary effectively.

3. Planning competency

  • Writing SMART learning outcomes, preparing lesson and unit plans, choosing appropriate activities.

4. Classroom management competency

  • Managing time, seating, discipline, large and mixed-ability classes; organising pair and group work.

5. Communication and interpersonal competency

  • Clear instructions, effective questioning, active listening, building rapport and a friendly environment.

6. Materials and ICT competency

  • Using and making teaching aids; using multimedia, audio-video, online resources and digital content.

7. Assessment competency

  • Designing reliable and valid tests, using continuous/formative assessment, rubrics and giving feedback.

8. Error correction and feedback competency

  • Correcting learners' errors sensitively using self-correction, peer correction and delayed correction.

9. Reflective and professional development competency

  • Reflecting on teaching, doing action research, attending training and learning continuously.

10. Personal and ethical competency

  • Patience, empathy, fairness, honesty, punctuality and commitment to learners' welfare.

11. Cultural and inclusive competency

  • Respecting diversity; supporting learners of different abilities, genders and backgrounds.

When an English teacher possesses these competencies, he or she can create a communicative, motivating and learner-centred classroom.

written.q: 4. (a) Describe the steps of teaching grammar in inductive approach.
written.a:
Inductive Approach to Teaching Grammar

In the inductive approach, learners are first exposed to examples of a grammatical structure in context. They observe the examples, discover the pattern and work out the rule themselves with the teacher's guidance. It moves from examples → rule ("rule-discovery"), the opposite of the deductive approach (rule → examples). It is recommended in CLT.

Steps of Teaching Grammar Inductively

  1. Warm-up / Setting the context: The teacher creates a situation or story using pictures, actions, realia or a short text in which the target structure occurs naturally. This arouses learners' interest.
  2. Presentation of examples: Several example sentences containing the structure are presented orally and then written on the board. Key parts may be underlined or coloured.
  3. Observation and analysis: Learners observe the examples carefully. The teacher asks guiding questions: "What is common in these sentences? When is the action happening? What form of the verb is used?"
  4. Discovery of the rule (generalisation): Learners, individually or in pairs/groups, try to find the pattern and state the rule in their own words. The teacher helps to refine it and writes the rule/form on the board.
  5. Checking understanding: Concept-checking questions and more examples confirm that learners have understood form, meaning and use.
  6. Controlled practice: Gap-filling, matching, sentence transformation and drills to practise accuracy.
  7. Free/communicative practice: Learners use the structure in meaningful communication — describing pictures, role-plays, writing short paragraphs.
  8. Evaluation and feedback: The teacher checks learners' performance and corrects common errors.

Advantages

  • Learners are active and think for themselves; rules discovered are remembered longer.
  • Grammar is learned in meaningful context.
  • Develops analytical and problem-solving skills.

Limitation

It takes more time and some learners may form wrong rules unless the teacher guides carefully.

written.q: 4. (b) How would you teach Present Continuous Tense to the students of class six following the inductive approach?
written.a:
Teaching the Present Continuous Tense Inductively (Class Six)

Class: Six   Time: 40 minutes   Topic: Present Continuous Tense

Learning outcomes: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to — (1) identify sentences in the present continuous tense, (2) form sentences using am/is/are + verb-ing, and (3) describe actions happening now.

Step 1: Warm-up and context (5 minutes)

The teacher greets the class and performs some actions: walks, writes on the board, opens a book. She asks a few learners to do actions — one stands and reads, two learners clap.

Step 2: Presentation of examples (7 minutes)

While the actions are happening, the teacher says and writes on the board:

  • I am writing on the board.
  • Rahim is reading a book.
  • Mina and Rina are clapping.
  • Look! It is raining outside. (using a picture)
  • We are learning English now.

Step 3: Observation and guided questions (6 minutes)

The teacher asks:

  • "Are these actions happening now or yesterday?" — Now.
  • "Which words come after I / Rahim / Mina and Rina?" — am / is / are.
  • "What is added to the verbs?" — -ing.
  • "Which word comes with 'I'? with 'he/she/it'? with 'we/they/you'?"

Step 4: Discovery of the rule (5 minutes)

In pairs, learners try to say the rule. The teacher then confirms and writes:

Subject + am/is/are + verb + ing + object

I → am; he/she/it/singular noun → is; we/you/they/plural noun → are. Used for actions happening now / at present. Signal words: now, at present, look!, listen!

The teacher also shows negative and question forms with examples: "Rahim is not sleeping." "Is Rahim reading?"

Step 5: Controlled practice (7 minutes)

  • Fill in the gaps: "She ___ (sing) a song now." "They ___ (play) football."
  • Picture task: learners write what people in a picture are doing.

Step 6: Free practice (6 minutes)

Pair work — "Guess the action": One learner mimes an action; the partner says, "You are swimming!" Then groups describe what is happening in the classroom right now.

Step 7: Evaluation and homework (4 minutes)

  • Oral questions: "What are you doing now?" "What is your teacher doing?"
  • Homework: Write five sentences about what your family members are doing in the evening.

In this way, learners discover the rule themselves from real actions and examples, which makes learning meaningful and lasting.

written.q: 5. (a) Discuss the importance of pronunciation in English Language.
written.a:
Importance of Pronunciation in English

Pronunciation is the way sounds, words and sentences are spoken, including vowels, consonants, word stress, sentence stress, rhythm and intonation. Good pronunciation is essential for effective communication in English.

Why pronunciation is important

  • Intelligibility: The main purpose of speaking is to be understood. Even with good grammar and vocabulary, poor pronunciation can make speech unintelligible.
  • Meaning distinction: In English, a small change in sound changes meaning — ship/sheep, live/leave, bat/bet, van/ban. Stress can also change meaning or word class: 'present (noun) vs pre'sent (verb).
  • English is stress-timed: Wrong stress and rhythm make speech sound unnatural and difficult to follow.
  • Intonation conveys attitude: Rising and falling tones show questions, surprise, politeness or certainty.
  • Better listening skills: Learners who know correct pronunciation can recognise words in native speakers' fast, connected speech.
  • Confidence: Good pronunciation increases learners' confidence and willingness to speak.
  • Positive impression: In interviews, presentations and international communication, clear pronunciation creates a good impression.
  • Academic and professional success: Tests like IELTS and TOEFL assess pronunciation; many jobs require clear spoken English.
  • Link with spelling and reading: Understanding sound–spelling relationships helps reading aloud and spelling.
  • Teacher as model: A teacher's pronunciation directly influences hundreds of learners; errors can spread and fossilise.

Conclusion: Pronunciation is not a decoration but a core part of communicative competence. Teachers should therefore give regular attention to sounds, stress and intonation from the beginning.

written.q: 5. (b) Make a list of diphthongs with an example for each one.
written.a:
Diphthongs in English

A diphthong is a vowel sound in which the tongue glides from one vowel position to another within the same syllable. In Standard British English (RP) there are 8 diphthongs. They are grouped into three types:

GroupDiphthongExample words
Closing — gliding to /ɪ//eɪ/day, make, rain
/aɪ/my, time, light
/ɔɪ/boy, coin, voice
Closing — gliding to /ʊ//əʊ/go, home, boat
/aʊ/now, house, cow
Centring — gliding to /ə//ɪə/here, near, ear
/eə/hair, care, there
/ʊə/poor, tour, sure

Summary list

  1. /eɪ/ — day
  2. /aɪ/ — my
  3. /ɔɪ/ — boy
  4. /əʊ/ — go
  5. /aʊ/ — now
  6. /ɪə/ — here
  7. /eə/ — hair
  8. /ʊə/ — poor

Note: English has 20 vowel sounds in total — 12 monophthongs (pure vowels) and 8 diphthongs.
